entities.summary:
The Kingdom of Naples, formally designated the Kingdom of Sicily on this side of the lighthouse (Regnum Siciliae ultra Pharum), was a significant political entity in the southern Italian Peninsula, spanning from its establishment in 1282 until its eventual absorption into the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies in 1816. Emerging from the division of the earlier Kingdom of Sicily during the War of the Sicilian Vespers, it controlled the mainland territories south of the Papal States, becoming a focal point for dynastic struggles between the Angevin, Aragonese, Habsburg, and Bourbon houses. Its strategic location and fertile lands made it a coveted prize, profoundly shaping the geopolitical landscape of the Mediterranean for over five centuries.

Following the 1282 revolt against Angevin rule on the island of Sicily, the mainland territories remained under Charles I of Anjou, thus forming the Kingdom of Naples. The Angevin dynasty held sway until 1442, when Alfonso V of Aragon conquered Naples, temporarily reuniting it with Sicily under the Crown of Aragon. After Alfonso's death in 1458, the kingdoms again separated. From 1504, Naples largely fell under direct Spanish Habsburg rule as a viceroyalty, a period characterized by significant cultural and economic exchange, but also heavy taxation and absentee governance. Following the War of the Spanish Succession, it passed to the Austrian Habsburgs (1714–1734) before becoming an independent Bourbon kingdom under Charles VII (later Charles III of Spain).

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Kingdom of Naples was a major regional power in the Mediterranean for over 500 years, influencing European dynastic politics and leaving a lasting cultural and political imprint on southern Italy that persists to this day.
